summary: The Clarendon Fund is Oxford's flagship graduate scholarship: over 200 new awards a year covering full course fees plus a living grant (at least £20,780 in 2025-26) for master's and DPhil students in any subject and from any country. There is no separate form: you are considered automatically when you apply to an Oxford course by its December or January deadline. Winners are usually top-of-class graduates (First Class or GPA 4.5/5 equivalent) whose application shows clear academic potential for the specific course.
lookfor: Outstanding academic achievement (typically First Class or equivalent)
Future potential and aptitude for the proposed course of study
Motivation and commitment shown in your statement and references
A strong departmental ranking: your department nominates its best applicants
cycle: For 2027 entry: apply to your Oxford course by its December 2026 or January 2027 deadline (course-specific); departments nominate in Feb–Mar 2027; most Clarendon offers go out by end of April 2027; if you have heard nothing by mid-June, you were not selected.

eligibility.q: Are you applying for a full-time or part-time master's or DPhil course at Oxford starting in 2027?
eligibility.no: Clarendon only funds graduate degree courses at Oxford. For undergraduate study look at Reach Oxford; for other UK master's look at Chevening or Commonwealth Scholarships.

eligibility.q: Can you submit your complete Oxford application by your course's December or January deadline?
eligibility.no: Applications made after the January deadline are not considered for Clarendon. Prepare now for the next year's December/January deadline.

eligibility.q: Do you have (or expect) a First Class degree or equivalent (for Nigeria, Oxford lists first-class honours, 70% or GPA 4.5/5)?
eligibility.no: You can still apply, but Clarendon is very competitive. A strong 2:1 (GPA 4.0/5) meets many Oxford course minimums; also look at need- or country-based awards such as Weidenfeld-Hoffmann or Chevening.

eligibility.q: Are you a new applicant (not already studying the same degree at Oxford and not holding a deferred offer)?
eligibility.no: Current students continuing the same degree and deferred offer-holders cannot be considered.

steps.title: Confirm that Clarendon fits you
steps.why: Clarendon is automatic, so your only 'application' is a very strong Oxford course application. Knowing this changes where you spend your effort.
do: Open the Clarendon page (link below) and read 'Information for applicants'.
Write down your degree class or CGPA and compare it with Oxford's Nigeria equivalents (first class = 70% or 4.5/5).
Note that there is no separate Clarendon form, essay or interview.
List 2–3 other awards you will also target (e.g. Weidenfeld-Hoffmann, Chevening, Commonwealth) as backups.
tips: Clarendon is merit-based, not need-based. Your grades, references and statement matter most.
avoid: Looking for a 'Clarendon application form' — it does not exist.
Assuming you can apply after the January deadline and still be considered.
check: I can say yes to: I know my course's funding deadline is my Clarendon deadline.

steps.title: Choose one Oxford course and note its deadline
steps.why: Departments nominate Clarendon scholars from their own applicants. A course that matches your background makes you rank higher.
do: Open 'Find your course' and search your subject.
On the course page, open the 'How to apply' tab and copy the exact December or January deadline into your calendar.
Note every document the course asks for: statement of purpose, CV, research proposal, written work, number of references.
Check the English level (standard or higher) and the minimum degree class.
If you apply to more than one course, check each deadline — each needs its own fee.
tips: Pick the course where your degree and experience clearly fit the entry requirements; a top-ranked applicant is more likely to be nominated.
avoid: Choosing a course only because it sounds prestigious when your background does not match.
check: I have one chosen course, its deadline, and a list of its required documents.

steps.title: Build your timeline and open the application
steps.why: Transcripts, English tests and references take weeks in Nigeria and elsewhere. Working backwards from the deadline prevents last-minute panic.
do: Open the Oxford graduate Application Guide and read 'Starting your application'.
Create your account on the graduate application form and start an application for your course.
In a calendar, set: referees asked (day -60), transcript requested (-60), English test booked (-75), statement final (-14), submit (-7).
Read the AI guidance: you may use AI for spelling and formatting, not to write your ideas.
tips: Aim to submit at least one week before the deadline; the portal is busy on deadline day.
avoid: Leaving the account creation until the final week.
check: I have an account and a dated timeline.

links.t: Using AI in your graduate application

steps.title: For a DPhil: study the department and possible supervisors
steps.why: Research applicants are judged partly on fit with available supervisors. A clear match makes a department more willing to nominate you.
do: Open the department website linked from your course page and read the research groups.
Pick 1–3 academics whose recent papers match your interest; read at least two papers by each.
If the course page invites contact, send a short email (under 200 words): who you are, your proposed topic, one link to your work.
Write the names of suitable supervisors into your application form when asked.
tips: Mention a specific paper or method in your email so it is clearly not a mass email.
avoid: Sending long emails with attached CVs to many professors at once.
check: I can name at least one Oxford academic whose work fits my proposal.

steps.title: Get your official transcripts
steps.why: An application without an acceptable official transcript is incomplete and may not be assessed in time for funding.
do: Go to your university's Exams & Records office (or its online transcript portal) and request an official transcript.
Ask for a scanned copy with stamp and signature, or an official e-transcript; Oxford accepts scans.
If you are still studying, request an interim transcript showing grades so far.
If any transcript is not in English, also get a certified English translation.
Save as PDF under 4 MB, clearly named (e.g. 'Surname_Transcript_BSc.pdf').
tips: Upload a portal screenshot only if it shows your name, institution, course title and all grades.
avoid: Typing up your own transcript in Word — it will be rejected.
Waiting until December: Nigerian registries often take weeks.
check: I have a legible PDF transcript under 4 MB showing every grade.

steps.title: Plan your English language evidence
steps.why: You can apply without a score, but you must meet the standard or higher level to take up a place, and a Clarendon award depends on meeting your offer conditions.
do: Check your course page: standard or higher level English.
Check if you qualify for a waiver: a full-time degree taught entirely in English completed within 2 years of your start date, or 2+ years' professional work in an English-speaking country.
If not, book IELTS (or another accepted test) in Lagos, Abuja or your city; one sitting must meet every component score.
Upload your score if you have it; otherwise state when you will take the test.
tips: Nigeria is not on the UKVI majority English-speaking list, so most Nigerian applicants need a test or a waiver.
avoid: Combining component scores from two different test sittings — Oxford does not accept that.
check: I know my English level, and I have a test date or a waiver plan.

steps.title: Write a sharp academic CV
steps.why: Assessors read your CV to judge your preparation for the course quickly.
do: Check if your course needs a CV and any page limit.
Order sections: Education (with class/CGPA), Research and projects, Publications/posters, Work experience (include NYSC), Awards, Skills.
Give one line of evidence per item (e.g. 'Final-year project: built X, graded A').
Export to PDF and name it clearly.
tips: Put your class of degree and rank (e.g. 'top 2 of 120') near the top — Clarendon is merit-based.
avoid: Photos, date of birth or long lists of unrelated hobbies.
check: My CV is a clean PDF that a stranger understands in 60 seconds.

steps.title: Write your statement of purpose
steps.why: This is the main place where you show 'future potential and aptitude' — the heart of Clarendon selection.
do: Copy the exact word limit and instructions from your course page.
Para 1: the academic question or problem you want to work on, and why it matters.
Para 2–3: your preparation — courses, project, research, work — each linked to the course.
Para 4: why this Oxford course and department (name modules, groups or academics).
Para 5: what you will do after, and how the course gets you there.
Ask one subject expert to read it; then cut every sentence that does not show ability or fit.
tips: Write about ideas and evidence, not about how much you love Oxford.
Use the course's own selection criteria as a checklist.
avoid: Exceeding the limit — over-length statements are removed and the application marked incomplete.
Using AI to draft — Oxford uses plagiarism checks and warns against it.
check: Every paragraph shows ability, preparation or fit.
I am within the word limit.

steps.prompt: Your research interests, academic background and career objectives, and why you are applying to the course (check your course page for exact instructions).
steps.limit: Set by each course — check the 'How to apply' tab

steps.title: For a DPhil: write your research proposal
steps.why: For research degrees, the proposal is the clearest proof of potential and feasibility.
do: Check the proposal length and format on your course page.
Use this structure: title; background and gap; research questions; methods; expected contribution; timeline; key references.
Show you know the field: cite 8–15 recent sources.
Link your proposal to the work of your chosen supervisor(s).
tips: Keep the scope realistic for 3–4 years.
avoid: A proposal so broad it reads like a literature review.
check: A non-specialist can state my research question after one reading.
steps.prompt: Your proposed research topic, questions and methods (check your course page).

steps.title: Secure three strong referees
steps.why: References weigh heavily in departmental rankings. Specific, enthusiastic academic letters push you up the nomination list.
do: Choose three people, mostly academics who taught or supervised you (e.g. project supervisor, HOD, a lecturer who knows you).
Ask each in person or by email 8 weeks ahead; send your CV, draft statement, course name and the deadline.
In the application form, register each referee with a working institutional email and set their deadline before your course deadline.
Track their status in the portal and send a polite reminder 10 days before.
tips: Ask referees to give a ranking (e.g. 'best student in 5 years') — Clarendon is about academic excellence.
Departments can start assessing once two references arrive, but aim for all three by the deadline.
avoid: Choosing a famous name who barely knows you.
Using a Gmail address for a referee when an institutional one exists.
check: All three referees are registered and have agreed.

steps.title: Sort out the application fee
steps.why: Your application is not submitted until the fee is paid or waived.
do: Note the fee: £75 for taught courses, £20 for research courses (card payment in pounds).
Check the fee-waiver list. Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya are not on the low-income country list, but many other African countries are.
If eligible, request the waiver at least two weeks before your deadline.
If paying from Nigeria, confirm your naira card allows international payments, or arrange a dollar/pound card.
tips: Test the card with a small international payment beforehand.
avoid: Requesting a waiver in the final week — late requests do not extend deadlines.
check: I know how I will pay or I have my waiver code.

steps.title: Complete the form and submit before the funding deadline
steps.why: Submitting by the December/January deadline is the only way to be considered for Clarendon.
do: Fill each section: Your details; References; Qualifications, languages and funding; Supporting documents; Declaration and payment.
In the Funding section, select any extra Oxford scholarships that need a tick box (Clarendon itself needs nothing extra).
Upload each document as PDF (under 4 MB), clearly named.
Proofread names, dates and grades against your transcript.
Pay and submit; save the confirmation email.
tips: Submit a week early; you can still track references afterwards.
avoid: Uploading Word files — only PDF, JPG or PNG are accepted.
check: I have a submission confirmation email.

steps.title: Prepare for a possible departmental interview
steps.why: Many courses interview shortlisted applicants online; a strong interview helps your ranking for nomination.
do: Re-read your statement and proposal; prepare a 2-minute summary of your research interest.
Prepare answers to: why this course, your best project, a challenge in your field, your plans after.
Test your internet, camera and a quiet room; have a backup data plan in case of NEPA/power cuts.
tips: Expect technical questions about your past work — know your own project deeply.
avoid: Memorised speeches; assessors want to see how you think.
check: I can explain my project and plans clearly in under 3 minutes.

steps.title: Watch for the Clarendon offer email
steps.why: Clarendon offers come separately from your course offer; knowing the timeline stops needless worry.
do: Accept your course offer and note its conditions.
Watch your email (and spam) — most Clarendon offers (letter 'CB1') go out by end of April.
Reply as instructed; a final funding breakdown letter ('CB2') follows between April and June.
If you have heard nothing by mid-June, assume you were not selected and use backup funding.
tips: Unsuccessful applicants are not contacted, so keep other applications alive until June.
avoid: Emailing the Clarendon office for updates before May.
check: I have accepted my course offer and know the conditions.

steps.title: Meet your offer conditions and get your visa
steps.why: Clarendon funding is secure only if you meet the conditions of your Oxford offer.
do: Send your final official transcript by 31 August (or your department's date).
Send your English test result if it was a condition.
Once Oxford issues your CAS, apply for the UK Student visa and book biometrics at the visa centre in Lagos or Abuja.
Plan flights and arrival for early October.
tips: Start the visa process as soon as you receive the CAS; summer is peak season.
avoid: Missing the 31 August final transcript deadline.
check: All my conditions are met and my visa is booked.

faq.q: Do I need to write a separate Clarendon essay?
faq.a: No. Submit your Oxford course application by the December or January deadline and you are considered automatically.

faq.q: Is Clarendon only for some countries?
faq.a: No. There are no nationality or residence restrictions.

faq.q: Will I be told if I am not selected?
faq.a: No. If you have not heard by mid-June, you were not selected.

faq.q: Does Clarendon pay for my family?
faq.a: No. It covers your course fees and a living grant for you only.

faq.q: Do I need IELTS before I apply?
faq.a: Not at the time of applying, but you must meet the level (or get a waiver) to take up your place.
